title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_χ$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_χ$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_χ$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_χ$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.

title: Resolving the thermal component of stellar feedback with the "anchor-and-refine" scheme in galactic simulations
comment: 11 pages and 8 figs in the main text; A&A in press
summary: (abridged) Stellar feedback regulates galactic baryon cycles, but galaxy-scale simulations often cannot resolve supernova cooling radii. Momentum-based subgrid models can consequently underresolve the hot gas around young stars. We develop an "anchor-and-refine" feedback scheme that anchors a host cell near each star particle, preventing its displacement and preserving a thermal-feedback reservoir. When the cooling radius is resolved, all supernova energy is injected into the host cell as thermal energy; otherwise, the host cell is refined and terminal momentum is deposited into surrounding gas cells. Idealized tests agree with high-resolution simulations, yielding consistent superbubble properties and preserving hot interiors without artificial cooling. In an isolated Milky Way-mass galaxy, the scheme captures finer X-ray-emitting structures and a sharply defined, X-ray-bright central mid-plane. It also produces a smoother star formation history than pure hybrid feedback. Hot gas dominates outflow mass loading, with the mass-loading factor plateauing at approximately 0.2 at heights z>1 kpc. Phase decomposition indicates that hot gas sustains a steady, energy-driven wind, whereas cooler outflows decline with height because of radiative cooling and gravitational fallback. These results highlight the role of thermal feedback in driving galactic winds. By preserving hot superbubble interiors and the partition of thermal and kinetic energy, anchor-and-refine improves the treatment of hot gas, star formation, and feedback at limited resolution, supporting future applications to galaxy-scale and cosmological zoom-in simulations.

title: Extra! Extra! X-ray Emission!: X-rays in Romulus25, Part II - Physical Drivers of X-ray Emission in the CGM
comment: 10 pages, 9 figures, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Characterizing the hot (T ~ 10$^{6}$ K) circumgalactic medium (CGM) around Milky Way-mass (MW-mass) galaxies is critical to a full understanding of galaxy evolution. In this second paper of the "X-rays in Romulus25" series, we unpack the specific physical processes giving rise to the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas in the halos of galaxies from the Romulus25 (R25) simulation, focusing on L$_{*}$ galaxies. We determine that a strong correlation appears between the mass of hot CGM gas, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, and the X-ray emissivity, $ε_χ$, measured in the first paper of this series, (Sanchez et al. 2026a, submitted). There is also a secondary correlation between M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$ and $ε_χ$ with the average metallicity of the hot CGM gas, $\bar{Z}_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. We use the well-studied PIONEER simulations from Sanchez et al. (2019), a set of zoom-in MW-mass galaxies run with the genetic modification technique of Roth et al. (2016) and the same physics as R25, to interpret these correlations. We determine that the presence of hot X-ray emitting gas is determined by two key processes: 1) the quantity of hot gas mass in the CGM, M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$, is set by the combined total energy injection of $both$ stellar and AGN feedback, and 2) together the average temperature and metallicity of the hot CGM changes the soft X-ray spectrum of the gas resulting in brighter metal-rich CGM and dimmer metal-poor CGM for the same quantity of M$_{gas, T > 10^{5.5} K}$. These results indicate, for the first time, that metal-rich gas halos may bias X-ray observations of MW-mass galaxies.

title: Not so dead after all: young stars in the massive S0 NGC 3115
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A, 12 pages, 6 figures, 2 appendix
summary: Context: Massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) are traditionally considered "red-and-dead" based on optical observations. However, ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy can uncover a hidden population of young stars with a sub-one-per cent mass fraction. Aims: We measure the young stellar mass fraction in NGC 3115, a massive isolated lenticular galaxy, to test the ubiquity and spatial distribution of this component beyond previously studied ellipticals. Methods: Using SOAR/Goodman spectra and line-strength fitting, we modelled the star-formation history with a single bulk stellar population plus a young component (constant star-formation over the last 1 Gyr). We used ultranest to derive posterior distributions for age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], and the young stellar mass fraction. Results: By tracking spatial variations in U-band indices, we found the young stellar mass fraction peaks at $0.69^{+0.09}_{-0.15}\%$ in the centre, dropping to zero beyond 1 kpc. This young component correlates with kinematic structures, dominating in the pressure-supported region. We interpret this as residual central star formation fueled by internal processes, such as recycled stellar material. Alternative UV-bright models (e.g., extreme horizontal branch stars) yielded poorer fits and unphysically high mass fractions. Conclusions: Young stars in old, "red-and-dead" galaxies are more common than expected. Their presence across various ETGs with similar gradients indicates that residual star formation is a ubiquitous feature, offering key constraints on the baryon cycle in these galaxies.

title: A double debris disc around a white dwarf sculpted by two planetary bodies
comment: 42 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in Nature Astronomy
summary: Many planetary systems survive the metamorphosis of their hosts stars into white dwarfs, as demonstrated by the detection of dusty circumstellar discs around these stellar remnants as well as chemical signatures of planetary debris in atmospheres of these stars. A small fraction of these circumstellar discs also contain gas, detected in the form of emission lines from various ionic transitions (most commonly the near-infrared Ca ii triplet). All of the 21 known gas discs exhibit double-peaked line profile characteristic of a rotating flat disc. The mechanism behind the the generation of gas is still debated, but for at least one system it has been linked with the presence of a surviving planetesimal embedded within the dust disc. Here we report the discovery of WD J132800.85-145019.95, a new gas disc system which exhibits quadruple-peaked instead of double-peaked line profiles. These emission lines originate from two separate gaseous rings extending from 0.14 Rsun to 0.34 Rsun and from 0.54 Rsun to 1.93 Rsun. We propose that this structure results from the presence of two distinct planetary bodies within these discs, ranging in size from a few km to the size of Pluto. The detection this stable double-disc presents a new challenge for the current models of debris disc formation and evolution.

title: Ejected and Rejected: Strong Scatterings in Dense Star Clusters
comment: Submitted to ApJ, Comments welcome!
summary: Understanding the evolution of collisional stellar systems is key to predicting both the bulk evolution of dense star clusters and also the rates of tidal disruption events, extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), stellar ejections, and other loss cone phenomena. Although a majority of the evolution is dictated by weak, small-angle scatterings, rare close encounters resulting in strong scatterings can sometimes produce qualitatively different outcomes. To systematically determine the astrophysical importance of strong scatterings, we derive the exact differential rate distribution of velocity kicks in isotropic and spherically symmetric distribution functions representing globular and nuclear star clusters, while also deriving the distribution boundaries and approximate rate scalings. We then extend this formalism to derive approximate rates of energy and angular momentum kicks for objects in the nuclear star cluster, and then apply this framework to study (i) ejections and (ii) ``cancellation'' of extreme mass ratio inspirals. We find that ejection rates are complicated in some regimes due to the saturation of the strong kick distribution and the breakdown of the weak limit, likely enhancing the effect of loss cone shielding. We also determine that a sizable fraction of proto-EMRIs will likely be canceled by strong scatterings, highlighting the need for future work to determine to what degree strong scatterings impact the true EMRI rate.

title: Machine learning applications in the heliosphere
comment: Review chapter submitted to the book Machine Learning Techniques for Astrophysics and Cosmology by Spring Singapore
summary: Space weather is the study of the near-Earth impact of the processes on the Sun. In a this era of technology, space weather emerges as a crucial area of study wherein the state of the near-Earth conditions need to be modeled and forecasted. Crucially, the advent of machine learning provides us with opportunities to study this subject in a rather comprehensive manner. In this chapter, we treat the the processes arising from Sun to the impact on the ground as a set of coupled systems, which can be studied in isolation or in a coupled manner. We define these individual systems in terms of their state vector $\vec{S}$, which provides us with an opportunity to define the physical variables determining the system. This also allows us to consider the systems in terms of their observables, obtained through the action of operators as $\vec{O}[\vec{S}]$. In such a formalism, the machine learning algorithms serve as {\it learned operators}, defined generally as inference ($\mathcal{I}$), propagation ($\mathcal{P}$), and emulation ($\mathcal{E}$). Through such a formalism, we present how machine learning helps advance our understanding of the physical systems under study, while also accelerating the development of operational models for space weather forecasting.

title: Simulation-Informed Dust Masses in Typical $6<z<14$ JWST Galaxies
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, submitted to ApJL, comments welcome
summary: Direct detections of dust in typical $z>8$ galaxies remain untenable, despite the presence of dust suggested by rest-frame UV/optical spectro-photometry. Informed by cosmological zoom-in simulations where dust particles evolve on-the-fly, we present a novel method for inferring dust masses in high-redshift galaxies using stellar half-light radii and UV/optical attenuation. Our methods reproduce observed trends at lower redshift, ultimately diverging from Milky Way-based calibration factors by up to $\sim1.5$ dex. We apply this method to observed JWST galaxies from $6<z<14$, and find dust masses in the range $M_{\rm dust}\sim10^3-10^5\,M_\odot$ that are fully consistent with upper limits from ALMA, and suggest an early dust enrichment period by supernovae followed by efficient grain destruction in the hot gas. Future observations may use our tabulated calibration to infer dust masses over a wide range of stellar masses and redshifts.

title: Probabilistic Stellar Mass and Radius Estimation with Bayesian Hierarchical Stacking
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, 5 tables. Accepted by A&A
summary: Accurate stellar parameters are essential for the characterisation of exoplanets, yet most host stars lack direct measurements of mass and radius. We aim to predict stellar masses and radii from commonly available observables and to quantify uncertainties and systematic effects in a way that is consistent with stellar observations. By not relying on a single model, we aim to obtain more robust predictive distributions and reduce sensitivity to model misspecification and outliers. We develop a Bayesian machine-learning framework that combines three probabilistic models through Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS): a Bayesian additive regression tree model, a two-process heteroscedastic sparse Gaussian process, and a hierarchical Bayesian neural network. The method propagates measurement uncertainties, accounts for correlations among inputs, and aggregates model variance into final predictive distributions. On a held-out test set the method attains a mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of 3.5% for mass and 2.1% for radius, improving on empirical-relation-based methods and standard machine-learning baselines. For 44 Kepler LEGACY stars, the BHS masses differ from estimates obtained with the BAyesian STellar Algorithm (BASTA) by a MARD of 4.8%, compared with 8.5% between the empirical relations and BASTA. Applied to about 2400 exoplanet host stars, the predictions differ from literature values by a MARD of 2.7% in both mass and radius. Residual analysis reveals mild underestimation for cool dwarfs, consistent with sparse training coverage, and positive offsets near the main-sequence turn-off that may reflect priors in isochrone-based catalogues. Internal consistency with g = GM/R^2 is greater for the BHS predictions, with a scatter in Delta log g lower by a factor of three than that of the literature values.

title: No Significant Excess in Typical Variability in CLAS+ Changing-Look AGN Candidates in Rubin DP2
summary: Rubin Data Preview 2 (DP2) samples the CLAS+ changing-look AGN (CLAGN) candidates $\sim1,000-9,000$ days after their comparison epochs, so it can test whether these objects retain enhanced short-term optical variability after their spectral transitions. Comparing peak-to-peak amplitude in magnitudes against a photometrically quiescent quasar control, one band at a time, we do not detect a significant median-amplitude excess for any state (turn-on, turn-off, intermediate) in either of two bands, nor a different in the median $\,|\,Δ\text{mag}\,|\,$ as function of time lag. The $r$-band CLAS+ amplitude distributions are wider than the control's, with the intermediate state formally significant after multiple-comparison correction. This could hint for a high-amplitude subpopulation.

title: Evolutionary Demographics of Molecular Ice Mantles in Young Stars with SPHEREx
comment: 25 pages, 8 Figures, 6 Tables. Manuscript submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Molecular ices are a primary reservoir of volatile C, O, and N in star-forming environments, tracing the chemical pathway from molecular clouds to planet-forming disks. SPHEREx provides contiguous 0.75--5~$μ$m all-sky spectrophotometry for vastly larger samples than are accessible to JWST, enabling population-scale ice demographics for the first time. We present a search for ice signatures in SPHEREx spectra of 20{,}292 young stellar objects (age $<20$~Myr) drawn from the Gaia-based kinematic catalog of Kounkel \& Covey 2019. Using laboratory templates for the spectral signatures of H$_2$O (3.05~$μ$m), CO$_2$ (4.27~$μ$m), and CO (4.67~$μ$m), we identify 746 H$_2$O ice candidates, including 131 high-confidence H$_2$O+CO$_2$ detections and 22 with additional corroborating CO absorption. When binning by age, we find that the H$_2$O$+$CO$_2$ detection rate declines by an order of magnitude between $\lesssim$3~Myr and $\sim$5~Myr, suggesting a chemical or physical evolutionary trend. Candidates concentrate toward high-extinction sightlines ($A_G \gtrsim 2.5$~mag) and embedded SED morphologies, consistent with the idea of envelope dispersal and photodesorption depleting detectable ice mantles within the first few million years of pre-main-sequence evolution. This catalog provides a homogeneous demographic baseline and a prioritized target list for JWST follow-up.

title: The Carousel Lens III: Joint lens convergence and source kinematic modeling
comment: 11 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables, submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: We introduce a new, independent modeling component to the Carousel Lens series by exploiting the spatially-resolved kinematics contained within the lensed arcs, which so far has remained rather underexplored in strong-lensing analyses. We present an end-to-end forward-modeling framework that reconstructs an integral-field spectroscopic datacube from a parameterization of the lens convergence profile together with the line-of-sight velocity, velocity dispersion, and surface brightness profiles of the unlensed source. The kinematic structure of the source acts as an additional set of ray-traceable markers distributed across every lensed image, inaccessible from imaging data alone. Furthermore, by generating an [OII] emission-line datacube, we isolate a single source redshift and remove lens and line-of-sight light contamination. We apply this framework to deep VLT/MUSE observations of the Carousel Lens, modeling the [OII] emission of the quadruply-imaged star-forming galaxy at $z_{\rm s} = 1.432$ that anchors the system's cosmography constraints. We measure an Einstein radius $θ_{\rm E} = 12.816''^{+0.005}_{-0.007}$ and a logarithmic slope $γ= 1.412^{+0.002}_{-0.002}$, tightening the statistical uncertainties on both by roughly a factor of $2-2.5$ relative to the corresponding flat emission-line map model. We find that the source galaxy exhibits a strong rotation, lies confidently along the star-forming main sequence, and has an inferred central black hole mass of $\log M_{\rm BH}/M_{\odot} = 7.89 \pm 0.51$. These results establish datacube-level forward modeling as a practical and independent route to traditional image-based lens models in the current systematics-limited regime, and one that extends naturally to this system's other lensed sources and to other lens systems.

title: Tayler Instability and Its Saturation in Rotating Stars
comment: Submitted to ApJ
summary: In stably stratified regions of rotating stars, magnetic instabilities play a key role by enabling dynamo and angular momentum transport. In particular, the Tayler instability of wound-up toroidal fields has long been considered to drive the Tayler-Spruit dynamo. However, the nonlinear saturation of the instability is poorly understood, despite its central role in the dynamo loop. In this paper, we use global simulations to verify the recently completed linear theory of the Tayler instability and determine its saturation. We confirm the picture of overstability of magnetostrophic and inertial waves, which grow on similar magnetostrophic timescales but oscillate with different frequencies. We find that magnetostrophic waves saturate with large amplitudes $δB/B\sim 1$ and dissipate the toroidal field on magnetostrophic timescales, while inertial waves saturate with $δB/B\ll 1$ and erode the toroidal field over much longer timescales. Moreover, magnetostrophic waves efficiently regenerate axisymmetric poloidal fields through nonlinear couplings while inertial waves do not. Our results indicate that the Tayler-Spruit dynamo can operate only through the magnetostrophic wave branch and that its steady-state may follow the scenario proposed by \cite{spruit2002dynamo}, ruling out the small-amplitude saturation scenario proposed by \cite{fuller2019slowing}. Implications for angular momentum transport and magnetic field amplification in evolving stars and nascent neutron stars are discussed.

title: Tidal shells as clocks of galaxy mergers and tests of cosmological models
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures; Proceedings IAU Symposium No. 403, The Hidden Beauty of the Galactic Outskirts
summary: Stellar shells-concentric arc-like tidal features formed in galaxy mergers-provide a valuable record of recent galaxy assembly histories encoding both the merger event and the gravitational potential of the host galaxy. We compare shell systems in observations and cosmological simulations from two complementary perspectives. First, we show that simulations predict a substantial population of very large (>100kpc) shells that are rarely observed, revealing a potentially important discrepancy between simulations and reality. Because the scales of observed and simulated shell systems differ significantly, we focus on a comparison of merger histories. Using a shell-identification method, we estimate merger times for a sample of nearby massive prolate rotators and compare them with merger histories derived from cosmological simulations. We also present ongoing efforts to expand the sample of deeply imaged prolate rotators using observations from the Milankovic telescope, paving the way for future studies based on larger observational samples.

title: Asteroseismic properties of young pulsators in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Discovery of period-spacing patterns in HD 281229
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Very young pulsating stars, including pre-main sequence pulsators, provide a rare opportunity to probe stellar interiors and investigate rotation during the earliest phases of stellar evolution. However, they remain relatively unexplored, particularly in the intermediate-mass regime. We aim to identify and characterise young pulsating stars in the Perseus Molecular Cloud using photometric data from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). We compiled Gaia-based membership catalogues for the Perseus Molecular Cloud, applied selection criteria to isolate young intermediate-mass stars, and extracted light curves from TESS full-frame images. Variability classification was performed using Lomb-Scargle periodograms and iterative pre-whitening. For confirmed pressure-mode pulsators, we estimated the frequency of maximum pulsation power, $ν_{\mathrm{max}}$. For gravity-mode candidates, we searched for period-spacing patterns and fit them using the traditional approximation of rotation. From 148 membership-selected targets, we identified eight pressure-mode pulsators and two objects showing possible gravity-mode pulsations. We analysed the previously known $δ$ Sct star V705 Per, bringing the total sample to 149 targets. One of the gravity-mode pulsators, HD 281229, is the youngest star known to date with a detected and modelled period-spacing pattern. By simultaneously fitting the dipole and quadrupole period-spacing patterns, we estimate an asymptotic period spacing of $Π_0=4776\pm400$ s and a near-core rotation frequency of $f_{\mathrm{rot}}=1.317\pm0.05$ $\mathrm{d}^{-1}$. These results highlight the potential of asteroseismology to probe the internal structure and rotation of very young stars. The detected period-spacing pattern in HD 281229 shows that gravity-mode asteroseismology can provide meaningful constraints on the properties of stars at early evolutionary stages.

title: Turbulent gas-rich discs at high redshift: Chaotic orbits and rapid bulge formation at high gas fraction
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Using the \nexus\ N-body/hydrodynamic framework, we show that stellar bars that emerge in high-redshift disc galaxies are different in their orbital characteristics compared to their low-redshift counterparts. We identify bar-supporting orbits and, among them, find the fraction of chaotic orbits compared to regular orbits ($f_{\rm chaos}$). This fraction rises above 60\% for models with $f_{\rm gas} > 60 \%$; for $f_{\rm gas} \lesssim 60\%$, we observe chaotic fractions close to zero. The emerging bars seen in the $f_{\rm gas}= 80\%$ and $100\%$ simulations collapse in $\lesssim$1 Gyr to form central bulges supported by rotation, and this collapse follows soon after the chaotic fraction starts to dominate ($f_{\rm chaos} \gtrsim 50\%)$. Moreover, the gravitational potential in those simulations steepens rapidly over that period, and by integrating the chaotic orbits, we find that orbits that deviate from the evolving mean field are more likely to be chaotic. Hence, we argue that the irregularity associated with the rapidly evolving, central potentials drives higher chaotic fractions in these gas-rich bars. As a result, the emergent bars collapse through `violent relaxation' to form oblate rotating bulges. Supporting evidence for this picture comes from the fact that particles of different mass share identical radial profiles, a natural consequence of the rapid relaxation process.

title: The Ubiquity of White-Light Flares on the Sun
comment: Submitted. Comments are welcome!
summary: White-light flares (WLFs) have long been considered rare on the Sun, as most magnetic reconnections occur in the corona, making it difficult to transport sufficient energy downward to heat the very low layers for WL continuum emission. However, it is also argued that WL continuum emission is a common feature of all flares, and the rare detection of them is largely due to the limited sensitivity and resolution of telescopes. Recently, we developed a new method to identify WLFs, which exhibits extraordinary detection capability. Combined with SDO/HMI's over 15 years of continuous photospheric observations, it provides us an unprecedented opportunity to address the long-standing debate about WLF ubiquity. A total of 1951 flares (547 B-class, 1316 C-class, and 88 M-class) from 769 low-activity active regions (ARs; flare number $<$ 10) observed during January 2011 - May 2025 are investigated. Among these, 1012 are identified as WLFs, giving an overall occurrence rate of 51.9\%. The occurrence rates for B-, C-, and M-class flares are 36.9\%, 56.9\%, and 85.2\%, respectively, showing a clear increase with flare class. The occurrence rate is also highly correlated with the AR's sunspot number. For the first time, we find that WL continuum radiation is widely present even among B-class flares. Different WLFs contain varying numbers of WL kernels, which exhibit distinct properties, evolutionary behaviors and different relationships with GOES soft X-ray flux and its time derivative. These results strongly suggest that WLFs are a common phenomenon on the Sun.

title: Unveiling the Shock-Excited Molecular Environment in the Orion Protostar HOPS 370
comment: 4 figures, 12 pages; accepted for publication in the Journal of Astrophysics and Astronomy (JoAA)
summary: We present near-infrared K-band ($1.94$--$2.52~μ$m) spectroscopy of the deeply embedded protostellar source HOPS\,370, obtained with the TIFR--ARIES Near Infrared Spectrometer (TANSPEC) on the 3.6-m Devasthal Optical Telescope (DOT). The spectrum is dominated by prominent molecular hydrogen ($\rm H_2$) ro-vibrational emission, with multiple transitions detected from the $1$--$0$ S, $2$--$1$ S, and $1$--$0$ Q branches. Using the intrinsically linked $\rm H_2$ $1$--$0$ Q(3) and $1$--$0$ S(1) transitions, which arise from the same upper energy level, we derive a visual extinction of $A_V = 23.24 \pm 1.25$ mag, corresponding to $A_K = 2.50 \pm 0.13$ mag, consistent with the embedded Class~0/I nature of the source. The diagnostic line ratio $F(2$--$1~{\rm S}(1))/F(1$--$0~{\rm S}(1)) = 0.12 \pm 0.01$ is consistent with thermal excitation and disfavors ultraviolet fluorescence as the dominant excitation mechanism. Assuming optically thin emission and local thermodynamic equilibrium, we derive an $\rm H_2$ excitation diagram that yields an excitation temperature of $2078 \pm 215$ K and a molecular hydrogen column density of $(1.93 \pm 0.93)\times10^{20}$ cm$^{-2}$. We further derive an ortho-to-para ratio of $2.45 \pm 0.21$, indicating substantial shock-driven thermal processing while remaining below the high-temperature equilibrium value of 3. Taken together, these diagnostics indicate that the molecular hydrogen emission in HOPS\,370 originates predominantly in warm, shock-heated gas most likely associated with its protostellar outflow. Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combined S- and Q-branch $\rm H_2$ spectroscopy for constraining the physical conditions and excitation history of deeply embedded protostellar systems.

title: Understanding the origin of silver in metal-poor stars based on the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium analysis of Ag I lines
comment: 12 pages, four tables, seven figures; accepted for publication in the Astrophysical Journal
summary: Silver is a poorly observed neutron-capture element, and understanding its Galactic production history requires accurate abundances for stellar samples covering a broad metallicity range. We refined the method for calculating stellar Ag abundances by considering the non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) line formation for Ag I. A comprehensive model atom of silver was built from the atomic data available in the literature, including recent data on inelastic Ag I + H I collisions. We derived abundances using the high-resolution spectra and the synthetic spectrum method with the one-dimensional model atmospheres. From two Ag I lines in the solar spectrum we obtained the NLTE abundances log epsilon = 1.15 and 1.10 for different treatments of collisions with hydrogen atoms. The NLTE abundances of Ag were determined for the first time for 41 stars in the -2.74 <= [Fe/H] <= -0.56 metallicity range. The NLTE abundance corrections for Ag I 3382 A were found to be larger for the giants (up to 0.92~dex) than the dwarfs (up to 0.51~dex). In NLTE, Ag in our sample stars is enhanced relatively to Fe and the [Ag/Fe] Galactic trend is very similar to that for [Eu/Fe]; the [Ag/Eu], [Ag/Ba], and [Ag/Sr] abundance ratios of the r-II stars CS22892-052 and CS31082-001 agree very well with the r-process model of Prantzos et al. (2020); the -1.6 < [Fe/H] <= -0.56 stars have close-to-solar [Ag/Eu] ratios. We conclude that production of silver was dominated by the main r-process throughout the metallicity range we investigated, with the main s-process contribution of not larger than 20% for [Fe/H] > -1.6.

title: Age-Resolved Vertical Motions in the Milky Way Warp: A Localized Enhancement in Intermediate-Age Populations
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 1 table, accepted for publication in ApJL. Online Dataset: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23308202
summary: Determining how the Milky Way warp evolves provides constraints on the formation and dynamical evolution of galactic disks. Using Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment Data Release 19 (APOGEE DR19) spectroscopy, we estimate ages for 222,355 red giants. With Gaia astrometry and geometric distances, we analyze 168,824 of these stars in five age bins spanning $0$--$10$ Gyr. The warp-related radial vertical-velocity ($V_Z$) profile of young red giants ($0$--$2$ Gyr) is broadly consistent with those of classical Cepheids and young open clusters. Over $9\leq R<12$ kpc, we find that the mean $V_Z$ values of the intermediate-age red giants ($2$--$4$ and $4$--$6$ Gyr) are $1.48\pm0.46$ and $1.49\pm0.52$ km s$^{-1}$ higher than that of the young population, respectively. By contrast, at $R\simeq12$--$13$ kpc, the $V_Z$ profiles of the $0$--$6$ Gyr red giants are consistent within their uncertainties. The intermediate-age enhancement persists across our robustness tests and may reflect smaller effective kinematic warp onset radii for the intermediate-age populations. The observed velocity differences may arise from the combined effects of earlier perturbations and the present-day warp, or from differences in vertical structure among stellar populations.

title: Atmospheric Parameter Determination of RR Lyrae Stars With Mephisto Multi-band Photometry
summary: Phase-resolved atmospheric parameters of pulsating stars, including RR Lyrae stars and Cepheids, are essential for studying stellar structure and pulsation physics and for establishing accurate stellar benchmarks for Galactic structure and assembly history. We present a photometric framework that simultaneously infers Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] from Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band (u, v, g, r, i, z) photometry. A supervised neural-network forward model is built by training on synthetic colors derived from theoretical stellar atmosphere models. It reproduces the synthetic colors to a precision of 0.01 per cent. The model is applied to observed multi-epoch colors to derive phase-dependent atmospheric parameters. We apply the method to six RRab and four RRc stars in three globular clusters observed with Mephisto. We find typical per-phase uncertainties of about 62 K in effective temperature (Teff), 0.10 dex in surface gravity (log g), and 0.16 dex in metallicity ([Fe/H]). Repeated measurements across the pulsation cycle reduce the typical formal uncertainty of the final [Fe/H] estimates to roughly 0.03 dex. A sensitivity analysis indicates that the five Mephisto colors provide distinct and complementary constraints on the three stellar atmospheric parameters: (u-v) provides robust constraints on log g, (v-g) is informative for estimating [Fe/H], and (u-v), (v-g), (g-r), (r-i), and (i-z) all provide information on Teff. The results demonstrate that Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band photometry can deliver precise, cost-effective phase-resolved atmospheric parameters for RR Lyrae stars, offering an efficient way to construct large samples of stellar benchmarks for studies of stellar pulsation physics and Galactic structure and evolution.

title: The Influence of Hubble Expansion on the Future Merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda
comment: 10 pages (+3 pages appendix). Resubmitted to ApJ after referee's report
summary: Most existing idealized simulations of galaxy mergers neglect Hubble expansion, as the local Hubble flow is curved by overdensities and the expansion effect is weak at these scales. However, even in the gravity-dominated Local Group (LG), the expansion itself still persists, and it has been shown important in some LG-related studies. Here we take the future merger of the Milky Way (MW) and Andromeda (M31) as a case study to investigate the differences between simulations with and without Hubble expansion. We perform a suite of idealized N-body simulations of the MW--M31 system under pure Newtonian, $Λ$CDM, and $w_0w_a$CDM scenarios, testing different masses and proper motions of galaxies informed by current observational constraints. At low M31 tangential velocities, especially in cases where the two galaxies merge within a Hubble time, the expansion effect is negligible; while at high velocities (>66.5 km/s), the $Λ$CDM simulations introduce a noticeable delay in the merger time compared to the Newtonian ones and may even alter the final fate of the system, but the caveat here is that the isolated-pair idealization and the assumed expansion history break down. The delay is also present but less pronounced in the $w_0w_a$CDM runs. When M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud are included, the differences in merger times are reduced. In summary, Hubble expansion can play a noticeable role for galaxy mergers with high tangential velocities, but its actual influence on the MW--M31 merger depends on the precise masses and proper motions to be determined in the future.

title: J060242.22+332452.7: hierarchical triple system with inner eclipsing contact binary
comment: submitted to AAS journals
summary: I present a discovery of hierarchical triple system J060242.22+332452.7. Inner contact binary system shows clear eclipse timing variation (ETV) due to light time travel effect (LTTE), with LAMOST medium resolution spectra reveals radial velocity (RV) changes of the third star. Joint fit of ETV and RV allows determination of outer orbit with period $P_{\rm out}=1866\pm6$ days and $e_3=0.40\pm0.05$. The masses are $M_{\rm AB,~C}\sin^3{i_3}=2.02\pm0.22,~0.86\pm0.08~M_\odot$. This system is expected to have an astrometric orbit in the next data release of Gaia.

title: GRAVITY-RESOLVE: A comprehensive image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations with GRAVITY
comment: Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A) on October 24, 2026
summary: We aim to improve and extend the imaging capabilities of the GRAVITY beam combiner instrument of ESOs VLTI with respect to reconstruction software in the Galactic Center. We revise and develop the image reconstruction code GRAVITY-RESOLVE $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, which has been specifically developed to reconstruct stars in the Galactic Center with GRAVITY. The main objectives are to increase the limiting magnitude in GRAVITY images, reduce its computational runtime, and allow for a joint reconstruction of multiple, spatially separate datasets/pointings on sky. We apply $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ to recent GRAVITY data, featuring the implemented GRAVITY-faint mode as part of GRAVITY+, the upgrade of GRAVITY. We reconstruct visibility phases and amplitudes and present the first GRAVITY image reconstructed with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ from these quantities. We demonstrate NIR mosaicking with $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ by jointly reconstructing nine separately acquired datasets of 2025 into a single image on a scale of $\simeq 3390\ \text{AU}\times 3390\ \text{AU}$, corresponding to $409.6\ \text{mas}\times 409.6\ \text{mas}$. With dedicated injection tests of point sources into GRAVITY data, we estimate the limiting magnitude to be $m_{\text{K}}\ \simeq\ 20.0$ within a radius of $25\ \text{mas}$ around the field center when reconstructing from closure phases and visibility amplitudes. We report on the discovery of two new faint stars in the Galactic Center: S303 and S304. Finally, we find a decrease in computational runtime by a factor of at least $\sim10$. With $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$, we demonstrate GRAVITYs capabilities for NIR imaging. We show that $\text{G}^{\text{R}}$ is a fast, precise, and deep image reconstruction tool for Galactic Center observations, enabling the discovery of even more faint stars.

title: Episodic Plasma Flows and Coronal Brightenings in an Arch Filament System Observed with SUNRISE III
comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Published in ApJL. Two animations are available with the online journal article
summary: Emerging flux regions (EFRs) transport magnetic flux and release energy in the solar atmosphere, often hosting arch filament systems (AFSs). We present high-resolution observations of an EFR obtained with Sunrise III, combining the Tunable Magnetograph (TuMag), the Sunrise Chromospheric Infrared Spectro-Polarimeter (SCIP), and the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The dataset follows an AFS continuously for nearly four hours. Line-of-sight (LOS) velocities derived from the Mg I b$_2$ line reveal three episodic plasma-flow events, with downflows reaching approximately 17 km s$^{-1}$ at the footpoints and enhanced upflows near the loop tops. Although this pattern agrees with the classical emergence and draining scenario, the strongest upflows and downflows occur nearly simultaneously. Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) observations at 304 and 171 Angstrom reveal transient extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) brightenings in the surrounding emerging system. Some occur during enhanced-flow episodes, while others do not, indicating that the temporal correspondence is not systematic. Multiline spectropolarimetric inversions reveal temperatures between approximately 4000 and 10,000 K and a smooth variation of magnetic field inclination along a representative AFS loop. Non-force-free-field extrapolations provide the large-scale magnetic context of the low-lying AFS loops and surrounding coronal structures. Together, the observations reveal a spatially and temporally complex evolution without establishing a direct causal connection between local plasma-flow enhancements and EUV brightenings.

title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
summary: The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four major spiral arms, including the Norma-Outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the "Norma arm" extending from one end of the Galaxy's central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. We now use a new generation of N-body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year old masers instead trace the Galactic bar's Quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust-lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the bar's parameters to be: a ~ 4.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, b ~ 2.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, phi = 20 (+5/-2) deg, Omega_p <~ 40 km s^-1 kpc^-1, representing the bar's semi-major and semi-minor half-lengths, inclination angle and pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way's spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

title: Infrared spectroscopy of the longest-period Galactic Mira variables from Palomar Gattini-IR: Identification of a candidate thermally pulsing Super-Asymptotic Giant Branch star
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures, submitted to PASP. Comments welcome!
summary: The population of extremely long-period Mira variables in the Milky Way remains poorly characterized. Their rarity and heavy circumstellar obscuration have precluded systematic studies in optical surveys, yet they are expected to trace the most massive stars evolving through the Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB). We present IRTF/SpeX spectroscopy of the longest-period ($P\gtrsim1000$ d) Galactic Mira variables identified with the Palomar Gattini-IR survey. Twelve of thirteen targets exhibit characteristics consistent with massive O-rich AGB stars. In contrast, one peculiar source IRAS 19552+3142 exhibits i) a large-amplitude ($ΔJ\gtrsim2$ mag) pulsations with $P\approx1060$ d, ii) strong C$_2$ and CO molecular bands indicating C/O$\gtrsim1$, and iii) SiC emission at $\approx11.3\,μ$m in archival mid-infrared spectra. Its spectroscopically confirmed chemistry makes it the longest period C-rich Galactic Mira variable known; together with the rarity of similar objects, this source is difficult to reconcile with standard massive AGB evolution where hot-bottom burning maintains an O-rich surface composition. Instead, its properties may be explained by super-AGB evolution where dredge-out episodes produce a C-rich surface and circumstellar material. Its high luminosity ($M_{[4.5]}\lesssim-10$ mag), red color ($[3.6] - [4.5]\gtrsim2.0$ mag), and high mass-loss rate ($\gtrsim 10^{-4} \mathrm{M_\odot yr^{-1}}$) resemble extreme AGB star progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients in nearby galaxies and a known chemically peculiar super-AGB star candidate in the Small Magellanic Cloud. IRAS 19552+3142 may thus provide a rare look at a Galactic super-AGB star in the thermally pulsing phase. Our results motivate improved theoretical predictions and long-baseline infrared searches for these short-lived, dust-enshrouded endpoints of stellar evolution.

title: Kinematic methods of spiral nature identification: limitations and applicability
comment: 17 pages, 11 figures, accepted in MNRAS
summary: The nature of spiral arms in galaxies remains debated, with several competing formation scenarios, including density waves, kinematic spirals, dynamic spirals, and recurrent modes, that are difficult to distinguish observationally. We tested two kinematic methods - the phase reversal method and the velocity harmonic dominance method - using toy models and mock data from TNG50 simulations. For bar resonances, the phase reversal method is strongly orientation-dependent and yields reliable corotation estimates only when the bar is aligned with the disc minor axis. For spiral arms, the phase reversal method does not always yield reliable results and should be used in tondem with another kinematic method. The velocity harmonic dominance method is more robust: it distinguishes between density wave, kinematic, and dynamic spiral patterns, although it still shows some sensitivity to orientation. Uncertainties in the rotation curve do not strongly affect its results. We also apply both methods to the observed grand-design spiral galaxy NGC3938 as an illustrative example; the results suggest the presence of multiple spiral modes, consistent with the recurrent modes scenario and this interpretation relies on different indirect evidence. Based on our findings, we propose a strategy for classifying spiral structure in observed galaxies that combines multiple independent tests. Applying this analysis to an extended sample will allow us to validate its predictive power and to investigate the diversity of spiral formation scenarios.

title: Rotation and outburst-like brightenings in ZZ Ceti stars observed by TESS
comment: 18 pages, 11 figures, 1 table available on CDS; accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary:
Context. Pulsating white dwarfs, such as ZZ Ceti stars, allow for the study of white dwarf rotation through rotationally split pulsation modes. Space-based photometry has also revealed outbursts in some cool ZZ Ceti stars.
  Aims. We extend the search for rotationally split pulsation multiplets and outburst-like brightenings among known ZZ Ceti stars observed by TESS. We check whether the TESS data add new evidence for a connection between outburst activity and stellar rotation.
  Methods. We analysed 120 s and 20 s cadence TESS light curves available up to Sector 96. After light curve correction and quality filtering, we performed iterative frequency analysis. Candidate rotationally split multiplets were identified automatically and visually validated. Outburst candidates were selected from smoothed flux excursions, followed by light curve inspection and pixel-level TESS diagnostics.
  Results. We identify 11 ZZ Ceti stars with accepted triplet candidates and derive rotation periods of about 8-94 h; three triplet detections are reported here for the first time. The targets are broadly consistent with the dispersion of rotation periods found in previous studies. The time-domain search produced 19 outburst-like events in 11 stars after light curve inspection. Pixel-level diagnostics indicate that most are likely caused by foreground asteroid contamination. We identify three stars (TIC 219442838, TIC 307908863, and TIC 630426257) as candidate stellar outbursters. None belong to the accepted triplet-rotation sample.

title: Chemodynamical Study and Evidence for Hot Compact Companions to Blue Straggler Stars in Berkeley 31
comment: 27 pages, including 14 figures and 4 tables, accepted for publication in the The Astrophysical Journal (ApJ)
summary: We present a detailed study of the open cluster Berkeley 31 using Gaia DR3 astrometry, Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy, and multi-wavelength photometry. We identify 329 probable cluster members from their proper motions and trigonometric parallaxes and use them to examine the cluster's fundamental parameters, stellar populations, and Galactic orbit. The cluster is located at a distance of $6024 \pm 181$ pc, with a color excess of $E(B-V)=0.148 \pm 0.047$ mag, and has a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] $=-0.36 \pm 0.04$ dex and $\langle [α/{\rm Fe}] \rangle=0.21 \pm 0.04$ dex. Isochrone fitting gives an age of $3.7 \pm 0.2$ Gyr, consistent with the independent chemical-clock estimate of $3.72 \pm 1.42$ Gyr. The systemic radial velocity is $57.89 \pm 0.08$ km s$^{-1}$. We find that about 38% of the MS stars are unresolved binary candidates with $q \gtrsim 0.5$. We identify 62 BSSs and 2 YSS candidates, including 48 BSSs and both YSSs not previously reported in the literature. We constructed multi-wavelength SEDs for these stars, including Swift/UVOT data for 28 BSSs. Two BSSs show clear ultraviolet excesses and are consistent with compact hot companions, one with a hot WD and the other with a pre-ELM WD. The present orbital parameters give a guiding radius of $12.29 \pm 0.29$ kpc and an eccentricity of $0.11 \pm 0.01$. Comparison with the estimated chemical birth radius indicates a moderate outward shift of the guiding center, with the present orbital position also contributing to the radial displacement. These results consistently describe Berkeley 31 as an intermediate-age, metal-poor outer-disk cluster and place its stellar populations in the context of its Galactic dynamical history.

title: The Bochum Survey of the Southern Galactic Disk: IV. Multi-Band Photometry
summary: The Southern Galactic Disk Survey (GDS) monitored a mosaic of 268 fields along a $6^\circ$-wide stripe in the southern galactic disk from September 2010 to September 2019. These fields were observed between 21 and 407 times simultaneously in $r'$ ($8\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim r' \lesssim 18\,\mathrm{mag}$) and $i'$ ($7\,\mathrm{mag} \lesssim i' \lesssim 17\,\mathrm{mag}$), supplemented by between 2 and 147 observations in each of the bands $U$, $B$, $V$, and $z'$. Here we present the matched multi-band catalogue, which integrates photometry and light curve data from all bands, containing photometry for almost 21.7 million Gaia DR3 sources, of which $113\,449$ are identified as variables. We give an overview of the survey's variable content with respect to its main characteristics and known variability type classifications. The comparison with the cross-match catalogue of Gaia DR3 sources with variables from the literature compiled by Gavras et al. (2023) and the International Variable Star Index (VSX) indicates that approximately $40\,\%$ of the variable sources remain unclassified in terms of variability type. Light curves for all of these sources are contained in the GDS data catalogues, available via the German Astrophysical Virtual Observatory (GAVO), and can contribute to their classification.

title: On The Scaling Relations Between Black Holes And The Galaxy/Bulge Mass And Their Connections With The Black Hole Occupation Fraction
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures. Submitted to ApJ, comments welcome!
summary: We investigate the black hole (BH)--host galaxy scaling relations predicted by the semianalytic model \texttt{FEGA25}, focusing on their dependence on BH mass threshold, galaxy morphology, and redshift, and on their connection with the BH occupation fraction (BHOF). Using the YS200 cosmological simulation as our reference volume, we study the $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ and $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\rm bulge}$ relations for different BH mass selections and compare their redshift evolution with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation \texttt{NewCluster}. We find that BH mass cuts primarily affect the low-mass regime, while the selected relations progressively converge toward the intrinsic no-cut relations at higher host masses. The $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ relation also depends systematically on galaxy morphology, with increasingly bulge-dominated systems preferentially occupying higher stellar masses. Over $z=0$--$3$, FEGA25 shows no clear systematic evolution of either scaling relation, consistent with a broadly preserved statistical connection between BH and host-galaxy growth. NewCluster shows no clear monotonic evolution either, although it exhibits larger scatter, particularly toward high host masses. We further show that BHOF and BH--host scaling relations encode complementary information. A low BHOF generally corresponds to a stronger selection-induced offset, but the mapping is not unique: substantially different occupation fractions can yield similar median scaling relations, and at fixed BHOF the bias depends on the host property and underlying BH mass distribution. At $z=0$, \texttt{FEGA25} is consistent with available observational constraints for both stellar- and bulge-mass relations, while predicting increased scatter and bending toward lower host masses.

title: A morpho-kinematic view of the Necklace nebula
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures and 2 tables. Accepted in MNRAS
summary: We present a morpho-kinematic study of the Necklace Nebula based on spatially resolved spectroscopic observations and 3D modeling performed with the SHAPE software. The nebula is characterized by an equatorial disrupted ring accompanied by bipolar outflows. The geometry and velocity field of these different components are derived from the comparison between observed and synthetic images and position-velocity diagrams. The best model successfully reproduces the main morphological and kinematic features of the nebula, allowing us to constrain its 3D structure. We confirm that the disrupted ring is tilted about 60° from the plane of the sky, but the bipolar outflows are inclined by 46° with respect to the line of sight. This situation might indicate that the bipolar structures are not simple extensions of the equatorial ring, but instead correspond to a distinct mass-ejection event. The slight misalignment between these two components suggests either precession of the ejection axis, a temporal change in the dominant mass-loss geometry, or a misalignment in the magnetic field. Given that the Necklace Nebula hosts a close binary central star and is a well-established post-common envelope planetary nebula, our results support a scenario in which binary interaction plays a central role in shaping its morphology, even before the common envelope phase.

title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.

title: Mg II Signatures of Frequency Dependent Wave Propagation in Magnetic Elements
comment: Submitted to Solar Physics. 22 pages, 4 figures
summary: Waves in solar magnetic elements provide a pathway for transporting and dissipating energy in the chromosphere, yet the relationship between photospheric oscillations and chromospheric spectral structure remains incompletely understood. We investigate whether distinct chromospheric Mg II spectral states are linked to different populations of photospheric kink mode oscillations, with particular focus on the role of high frequency (~5mHz) waves. Magnetic elements are tracked in SDO/HMI magnetograms to derive horizontal velocity power spectra, while corresponding Mg II h + k profiles from IRIS are classified using k-means clustering into morphology-based (SHAPE) and intensity-based (ABS) groups. Both classifications exhibit systematic differences in oscillatory behavior. The SHAPE clusters isolate spectral morphologies associated with enhanced high-frequency power, including cases where oscillations in the 4-6 mHz band exceed those in the photospheric p-mode band. In contrast, the ABS clusters show a monotonic increase in the relative contribution of high-frequency oscillations with increasing emission strength and magnetic flux. These results indicate that high-frequency oscillations are both selectively enhanced in specific chromospheric states and systematically strengthened in stronger magnetic environments. This suggests that magnetic structuring plays a key role in regulating both the transmission and the conversion of kink mode wave energy into observable chromospheric signatures.

title: ARRAKIHS: The observability of tidally stripped satellites in a Milky Way-like halo
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: Deep imaging surveys are revealing increasing numbers of low surface brightness stellar streams around Milky Way-like galaxies. These streams trace the orbital evolution and internal structure of their disrupted dwarf galaxy progenitors. We investigate the evolution and observability of tidal features from dwarf galaxies consistent with the $Λ$CDM framework and Local Group observations. We performed high-resolution $N$-body simulations of dwarf galaxies orbiting in a static Milky Way-like potential comprising a disc, bulge, and dark matter halo. Each dwarf comprised a Plummer stellar distribution embedded in a cuspy or cored generalised Navarro--Frenk--White dark matter halo. Idealised integrated surface brightness maps were constructed every 0.5 Gyr over 10 Gyr, and detectability was quantified through the projected area of stellar light brighter than limiting surface brightnesses, $μ_{\rm lim}=29$--$32$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$, chosen to span depths relevant to ARRAKIHS, LSST, and Euclid. The detectability of tidal features depends most strongly on progenitor stellar mass, orbital configuration, parameterised by the eccentricity proxy $e_0$, and evolutionary stage. Across this range, extended tidal debris is predominantly recovered for initially more radial configurations, mainly those with $e_0 \gtrsim 0.75$. In the simulated grid, detectable area is dominated by $M_\star=10^8$--$10^9 M_\odot$ progenitors, whereas $M_\star=10^6$--$10^7 M_\odot$ systems can undergo stripping without detectable debris. The detectable area evolves non-monotonically with time, reflecting the competition between stream formation, phase mixing, and the fading of diffuse debris below the adopted surface brightness limits. Cuspy and cored progenitors show similar evolution of the detectable area, with differences smaller than the scatter induced by orbital diversity.

title: A Low-Dimensional Chemical Representation of High-Resolution Stellar Disk Spectra: Residual Abundance Signatures
comment: 32 pages, 41 figures
summary: Stellar abundances are generated by complex chemical enrichment pathways yet show strong correlation structure. We test how well high-quality spectra of low-alpha disk stars can be reconstructed using low-dimensional models. By validating model performance in flux space, we quantify and locate where residual information persists. Using HARPS spectra (R = 115,000, SNR > 100) and labels derived with Korg, we train generative models (The Cannon) conditioned on stellar parameters Teff, log(g), [M/H], vsini, and vmic, and three abundance labels, [Ti/H], [Y/H], and [Nd/H], representing distinct nucleosynthetic families. Evaluating model performance on unseen test stars through flux residuals, the model reproduces the global spectra to a median residual amplitude of 0.3%. Deviations in 15 absorption features for unlabelled elements are typically < 0.7%. Residuals of ~1% correspond to abundance differences of 0.01-0.05 dex. Degrading the spectra to medium resolution (R = 28,000) decreases the median residual amplitude from 0.3% to 0.2%, redistributing the residual signal over the instrumental line profile. Our publicly available model reproduces features from 29 elements to sub-percent precision across -1.13 < [M/H] < 0.29. This demonstrates that the dominant chemical variation encoded in low-alpha disk spectra can be captured by a low-dimensional model, while weaker chemical information remains encoded in flux residuals. High-resolution, high-SNR spectra (R ~ 100,000, SNR > 100) are essential to resolve the hierarchical layers of chemical information beyond this low-dimensional structure. The model provides a benchmark for assessing the chemical information accessible to current surveys like 4MOST and GALAH 2, as well as upcoming facilities like VLT/HRMOS and GMT/G-CLEF.

title: The extragalactic science of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen spectroscopic survey II: Discovery of a galaxy cluster at z = 0.089 behind the Galactic plane
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Letter accepted for publication in A&A
summary: The Zone of Avoidance (ZoA) continues to represent the most significant incompleteness in the extragalactic census of the Local Universe. It is evident that photometric surveys alone are insufficient to establish whether the galaxy overdensities detected therein are physical systems or projections along the line of sight. We present the first spectroscopic results of the extragalactic science area of the KMOS VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, demonstrating how near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy can reveal and dynamically characterise galaxy clusters hidden by the Milky Way. A photometric overdensity of 19 galaxy candidates was identified in the VVV NIRGC III catalogue, centred at $(l,b)=(274.05^\circ,+2.85^\circ)$ with a mean interstellar extinction of $A_{K_s}=0.2$ mag; 16 of these candidates were observed with VLT/KMOS in the $HK$ grating and yielded spectra with reliable cross-correlation radial velocities. A total of 14 galaxies form a compact structure with a mean redshift of $\langle z \rangle = 0.089 \pm 0.001$, which corresponds to a mean radial velocity $\langle cz \rangle = 26660 \pm 170$ km/s, while two are foreground galaxies. The rest-frame line-of-sight velocity dispersion is $σ_v = 560^{+110}_{-120}$ km/s, implying an indicative dynamical mass of $M_{200} = 1.9^{+0.7}_{-1.1} \times 10^{14} M_\odot$ (based on members within the cluster core $\sim 0.4 r_{200}$) and placing the system in the poor-cluster regime. Of these 14 cluster members, 13 also lie within the $2σ$ scatter of the fitted near-IR red sequence. The other two galaxies are foreground objects that lie outside this range.

title: Insights into the Kinematic Evolution of Filament-Induced Jets: Coupling of Interchange and Flare Reconnection
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Jets are ubiquitous eruptive activities in the solar atmosphere, playing an important role in mass transport, atmospheric heating, and energy supply. However, the triggering mechanism remains elusive. To reveal the fine process of jet evolution, we study a jet associated with a B-class flare that involves in two distinct stages. Analyzing the complete evolution of a solar jet captured by the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO), we clearly identify its dual-stage kinematics, evolving from interchange to flare reconnection. This dual-stage jet is characterized by distinct dual-stage signatures in magnetic morphology, H$α$ profile, jet speed, jet height, X-ray flux, loop-top source, and temperature. These differences are naturally unified by a physical picture coupling interchange and flare reconnection, offering new insights into understanding of the physical process of filament-induced jets.

title: Environmental Quenching of Satellite Galaxies out to z~0.4 with GAMA and DEVILS
comment: 22 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: While numerous studies have shown that satellite galaxies experience declining star formation rates after infall, direct comparisons across different surveys and redshifts are complicated by varying sample selections, environmental metrics, and techniques used to derive galaxy properties. In this work, we select satellite galaxies from the highly complete Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey and the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) to investigate environmental quenching out to z~0.4. These surveys derive galaxy properties and environments in a consistent manner, minimizing systematic biases and enabling a robust comparison across redshift. Using projected phase space as a proxy for infall time, we quantify the evolution of the quenched fraction and trace how satellites evolve relative to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). We find consistent trends between GAMA and DEVILS, with satellites exhibiting a steady decline in star formation relative to the SFMS at a rate of ~0.14 dex/Gyr following infall. Extending this analysis to include visual morphology, we find similar declining trends for both early- and late-type systems. Overall, we find no significant redshift evolution between GAMA and DEVILS, indicating that group and cluster environments have a comparable impact on the star formation activity of satellite galaxies over the past ~4.5 Gyr.

title: The Pointing Error Due To Laser Propagation in Space Plasma for TianQin Gravitational Wave Detection
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures Published in Space Weather
summary: TianQin, a space-borne gravitational wave observatory, is designed to detect gravitational-wave signals via laser interferometry. As the inhomogeneous space plasma surrounds the inter-satellite laser links, the propagation of the laser in space plasma can introduce pointing error noise. In this work, we quantitatively assess the effect of plasma on the pointing accuracy of TQ's inter-satellite laser links. We employ a magnetohydrodynamic model to simulate the plasma distribution around the TQ orbit for different orbital orientations. Using the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method to conduct the ray-tracing calculations over a TQ orbital cycle under a solar wind dynamic pressure close to the 23-year average, we find that the plasma-induced laser deflection angle and pointing eccentricity are on the order of $10^{-20} \ \mathrm{rad}$ and picometers, respectively. These values are significantly lower than TQ's requirements. Our results demonstrate that the impact of space plasma on TQ's pointing error is negligible in moderate space weather conditions, indicating a positive outlook for the TQ mission.

title: Odds Estimation for Supermassive Black Hole Binaries in Local Core Galaxies
comment: 18 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables, submitted to AAS Journals
summary: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs) are expected products of massive galaxy mergers, but identifying binaries in nearby galaxies remains challenging. We combine simulated massive-galaxy assembly histories from IllustrisTNG with a semi-analytic core-scouring model to connect observable core galaxy properties to the probability of hosting a bound SMBHB at z=0. We (i) construct a core galaxy population using an observationally motivated galaxy stellar mass function, (ii) model binary evolution through dynamical friction, stellar hardening, and gravitational-wave emission, and (iii) perform logistic regressions with five observable predictors: stellar mass deficit, stellar mass, central density, central velocity dispersion, and effective radius. The resulting models perform well on simulated systems, achieving a pseudo-$R^2$ of $0.51\pm0.03$, accuracy $0.95\pm0.01$, precision $0.92\pm0.03$, and recall $0.82\pm0.04$. Uncoalesced binaries are typically compact, with separations peaking near 0.3 pc, though only $\sim0.3\%$ emit in the pulsar timing array band. Applying the model to observed core galaxies, we identify eight nearby galaxies more likely than not to host SMBHBs. Of those eight host candidates, we note Messier 86 (NGC 4406) as a particularly likely example that was similarly identified using independent means and therefore warrants future follow-up.

title: Energy-Dependent Hard X-Ray QPP Modulation in M- and X-Class Solar Flares Observed by Aditya-L1/HEL1OS
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 1 table
summary: Quasi-periodic pulsations (QPPs) in solar-flare hard X-ray (HXR) emission provide observational constraints on the temporal variability of flare energy release and energetic-electron production. In our previous study, we established a systematic catalogue of HXR QPPs in HEL1OS observations of X-class solar flares, identifying statistically significant pulsations in 25 of 34 events with sufficient data quality (S. Rajkapoor Kanaujiya et al. 2026). Here, we extend this investigation by comparing the energy dependence of the modulation depth of QPPs in M- and X-class flares across four HEL1OS energy channels spanning 8-20 keV. The comparison comprises 18 M-class events and the X-class sample from our previous study, with the number of available measurements varying between energy channels. title: Detailed chemo-dynamical characterization of four elusive Milky Way star clusters
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: A variety of faint and observationally challenging stellar systems has been discovered in the Milky Way in the last decades. title: Recent advances in numerical modeling of solar inertial modes
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures; Accepted for publication in Solar Physics
summary: Inertial modes are low-frequency global oscillations in rotating fluids, restored by the Coriolis force. The amplitudes of linearly stable modes can be estimated from their response to stochastic forcing, whereas those of linearly unstable modes must be determined using nonlinear numerical modeling. We further discuss the possible dynamical roles of large-amplitude inertial modes in transporting heat and angular momentum in the Sun. title: 3-Methoxy-1-propanol Rotational Spectroscopy and Radio Astronomical Search toward NGC 6334I
summary: The methoxy functionalized alcohol species methoxymethanol and 2-methoxyethanol have recently been identified toward the MM1 protostellar source in the NGC 6334I massive star-forming region. Here we report measurements of portions of the centimeter, millimeter, and sub-millimeter regions of the rotational spectrum of the most stable conformer of 3-methoxy-1-propanol in order to probe the presence of even larger methoxylated alcohols toward the source. The experimental rotational parameters determined from these spectra were used to simulate the rotational spectrum of 3-methoxy-1-propanol under the physical conditions of the MM1 source and compared to the same ALMA observational dataset of the source in which 2-methoxyethanol was first discovered. No 3-methoxy-1-propanol transitions are identified in the data, and an upper limit on its column density toward the source was determined to be $7.5 \cdot 10^{15} \text{ cm}^{-2}$. When considering the series of these three methoxy alcohols, the decrease in column density going from 2-methoxyethanol to 3-methoxy-1-propanol is consistent with how the column density of 2-methoxyethanol decreases compared to methoxymethanol.

title: Analysis of Multi-Wavelength Data for 30 Galactic Emission-Line Stars with Dusty Envelopes
comment: 21 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables
summary: We selected 30 stars with V-band brightnesses of 11-16 mag, visual color-indices B-V of approximately 1.3 mag or less, and large near-IR color-indices (J-H and H-K of approximately 0.7 mag or greater) to search for the presence of the B[e] phenomenon. Spectroscopic observations confirmed the presence of emission lines previously detected in 11 stars of the sample and revealed them in 4 other stars for the first time. Spectral energy distributions (SEDs) in the optical and IR spectral regions were analyzed and compared with theoretical SEDs. The fundamental parameters were estimated using the SED fits corrected for the interstellar and circumstellar (CS) extinction and Gaia DR3 distance measurements. Properties of 14 objects previously classified as pre-main-sequence stars were reevaluated. The B[e] phenomenon was found in 16 objects, most of which exhibit observed properties of FS CMa type objects, a still small group of Galactic stars or binary systems with predominantly hot CS dust. The nature and evolutionary status of 11 sample objects remain uncertain and require further investigation.

title: The origin of UV emission in extremely low-mass satellite galaxies: Insights from Leo T
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Leo T, a Milky Way (MW) satellite, is the lowest-mass gas-rich galaxy known to show recent star formation, making it an excellent laboratory for investigating star formation in the ultraviolet (UV) regime within a low-density, metal-poor environment. We extracted thirty SFCs and derived their properties, including area, luminosity, and star formation rate (SFR), and compared them with previous studies. We find that five out of the six FUV-emitting stars with MUSE spectroscopy are extremely metal-poor ([Fe/H] $\leq$ -3). The (NUV - r) color profile indicates that the UV emission is dominated by stellar populations younger than 1 Gyr out to a radius $\lt$ 185 pc. Despite the recent detection of CO(1-0) emission, no SFCs are associated with the molecular clouds, which exhibit extremely low SFEs. The spatial distribution of the SFCs suggests a directional interaction with the MW.

title: Four-hundred Very Metal-poor Stars Studied with LAMOST and Subaru. IV. Heavy Element Enhanced Stars
comment: 26 pages, published in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: We perform a homogeneous analysis of 82 heavy-element-enhanced metal-poor stars from the\\ LAMOST/Subaru sample, including 64 $r$-process-enhanced stars, 2 limited-$r$ stars, and 16 stars exhibiting significant or moderate carbon enhancement (comprising 9 $s$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$/$s$, and 3 $r$+$s$ stars). We identify an extremely metal-poor $r$-II star, J1158+0734 ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]}$ = -2.93), whose enhanced Zn abundance ($\mathrm{[Zn/Fe]}$ = +0.67) is best explained by yields from a high-energy, massive core-collapse supernova. title: Probing Multi-formation Channels of Dark Matter-Deficient Galaxies in a Simulated Universe
comment: 28 pages, 21 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: We investigate the formation and evolution of dark matter-deficient galaxies (DMDGs) using the IllustrisTNG100 cosmological hydrodynamical simulation. In the second, galaxies form with little or no dark matter from the beginning (inborn DMDGs). The two populations show distinct physical properties. Acquired DMDGs exhibit significant temporal variations in mass content, size, and kinematics, whereas inborn DMDGs show mild evolution. The former population tends to form closer to their nearest neighbor galaxies in large-scale overdense regions than the latter population does. We find that most stars in the inborn DMDGs form in situ. Their precursor gas is already metal-enriched and associated with other galaxies before formation. Tidal interactions and filamentary gas flows may contribute to the assembly of compact gas clumps, suggesting multiple formation pathways for inborn DMDGs. Our findings support the idea that there are at least two distinct channels to make galaxies dark matter deficient, which is important for understanding the formation mechanisms of these extreme systems.

title: Nine new eclipsing accreting ultracompact white dwarf binaries from the Zwicky Transient Facility
comment: to be submitted to A and A, comments welcome
summary: Accreting ultracompact white dwarf binaries (accreting UCBs) transfer helium-rich material at orbital periods below about 65 min, and mainly divide into hydrogen-free AM CVn binaries and helium cataclysmic variables.
